claim: Direct striatal manipulations such as self-stimulation of direct-pathway projection neurons (dMSNs) are sufficient to induce reinforcement within minutes.
source: Indeed, direct striatal manipulations such as self-stimulation of direct-pathway projection neurons (dMSNs) are sufficient to induce reinforcement within minutes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work and is consistent with the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mimicking the effects of dMSN activation on downstream circuitry through optogenetic suppression of substantia nigra reticulata (SNr) is sufficient to drive rapid reinforcement.
source: We found that mimicking the effects of dMSN activation on downstream circuitry, through optogenetic suppression of basal ganglia output nucleus substantia nigra reticulata (SNr) or activation of SNr targets in the brainstem or thalamus, was also sufficient to drive rapid reinforcement.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing SNr self-inhibition behavior in Figure 3.

claim: Activation of SNr targets in the brainstem or thalamus is sufficient to drive rapid reinforcement.
source: We found that mimicking the effects of dMSN activation on downstream circuitry, through optogenetic suppression of basal ganglia output nucleus substantia nigra reticulata (SNr) or activation of SNr targets in the brainstem or thalamus, was also sufficient to drive rapid reinforcement.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing self-stimulation of VM, DRN, and MLR in Figure 3.

claim: Silencing motor thalamus is the only manipulation that reduced dMSN-driven reinforcement among selected targets of SNr.
source: Remarkably, silencing motor thalamus—but not other selected targets of SNr—was the only manipulation that reduced dMSN-driven reinforcement.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5 showing that VM silencing reduced dMSN self-stimulation while DRN and MLR silencing did not.

claim: Basal ganglia output to motor thalamus plays an unexpected role in striatum-driven reinforcement.
source: Together, these results point to an unexpected role for basal ganglia output to motor thalamus in striatum-driven reinforcement.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings showing VM is necessary for dMSN-driven reinforcement.

claim: Standard models of reinforcement invoke dopamine-dependent corticostriatal plasticity as a mechanism underlying associative learning.
source: Standard models of reinforcement invoke dopamine-dependent corticostriatal plasticity as a mechanism underlying this form of associative learning (Schultz and Dickinson, 2000; Reynolds et al., 2001; Doya, 2007; Maia and Frank, 2011; Yagishita et al., 2014; Xiong et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Activating targets of basal ganglia output can be reinforcing.
source: Yet other studies have found that activating targets of basal ganglia output can also be reinforcing (classic electrical studies reviewed in Wise, 1996); for recent optogenetic studies, see below)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Reinforcement learning in songbirds and primates is proposed to involve basal ganglia regulation of cortical plasticity.
source: and reinforcement learning in songbirds and primates is proposed to involve basal ganglia regulation of cortical plasticity (Turner and Desmurget, 2010; Fee and Goldberg, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Direct pathway medium spiny neurons (dMSNs) increase movement.
source: The striatum contains two distinct classes of projection neurons—direct (dMSNs) and indirect pathway medium spiny neurons (iMSNs)—that regulate motivated behavior by increasing or suppressing movement, respectively (Albin et al., 1989; Kravitz et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Indirect pathway medium spiny neurons (iMSNs) suppress movement.
source: The striatum contains two distinct classes of projection neurons—direct (dMSNs) and indirect pathway medium spiny neurons (iMSNs)—that regulate motivated behavior by increasing or suppressing movement, respectively (Albin et al., 1989; Kravitz et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Striatal stimulation is sufficient to drive operant responding in rodents in the absence of food reward.
source: Early intracranial self-stimulation experiments showed that striatal stimulation is sufficient to drive operant responding in rodents, in the absence of food reward (Phillips et al., 1976; White and Hiroi, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Striatal microstimulation biases choice in cue-guided decision tasks in primates.
source: In addition, striatal microstimulation biases choice in cue-guided decision tasks in primates (Nakamura and Hikosaka, 2006; Williams and Eskandar, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Direct pathway stimulation is reinforcing.
source: Although some of these effects are due to dopamine release from axon stimulation, pathway-specific optogenetic stimulation later revealed that direct pathway stimulation is reinforcing, whereas indirect pathway stimulation drives avoidance (Hikida et al., 2010; Kravitz et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Indirect pathway stimulation drives avoidance.
source: Although some of these effects are due to dopamine release from axon stimulation, pathway-specific optogenetic stimulation later revealed that direct pathway stimulation is reinforcing, whereas indirect pathway stimulation drives avoidance (Hikida et al., 2010; Kravitz et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mice readily learned an operant task to self-stimulate dMSNs and formed a memory of the stimulation-paired apparatus.
source: Indeed, mice readily learned an operant task to self-stimulate dMSNs and formed a memory of the stimulation-paired apparatus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Kravitz et al., 2012) and data in the current manuscript.

claim: dMSN stimulation is not just acutely rewarding but can drive long-lasting changes in the brain supporting learning and memory.
source: This suggests that dMSN stimulation is not just acutely rewarding but can drive long-lasting changes in the brain supporting learning and memory (Kravitz et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and inference from the data.

claim: Stimulation of direct and indirect pathways oppositely biases both choice and vigor in water-reinforced tasks.
source: Consistent with this, stimulation of direct and indirect pathways oppositely biases both choice and vigor in water-reinforced tasks (Tai et al., 2012; Yttri and Dudman, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In vivo recordings from primates and rodents show that activity in discrete populations of MSNs encodes reward.
source: Similarly, in vivo recordings from primates and rodents show that activity in discrete populations of MSNs encodes reward (Hikosaka et al., 1989; Apicella et al., 1991; Oyama et al., 2010), actions and/or their values (Lauwereyns et al., 2002; Barnes et al., 2005; Pasupathy and Miller, 2005; Samejima et al., 2005; Lau and Glimcher, 2008; Kim et al., 2009; Kimchi and Laubach, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: MSNs both integrate and support motor and reinforcement functions.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that MSNs both integrate and support motor and reinforcement functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the cited literature.

claim: The superior colliculus is implicated in orienting.
source: Different brainstem targets of basal ganglia are associated with regulation of distinct aspects motor behavior: the superior colliculus is implicated in orienting (Hikosaka et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The periaqueductal gray is involved in freezing.
source: the periaqueductal gray is involved in freezing (Gross and Canteras, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The mesencephalic locomotor region (MLR) is engaged for locomotion.
source: and the mesencephalic locomotor region (MLR) is engaged for locomotion (Esposito and Arber, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Dorsal Raphe Nucleus (DRN) neurons are involved in mood regulation and state-dependent control of motivation.
source: whereas Dorsal Raphe Nucleus (DRN) neurons are involved in mood regulation and state-dependent control of motivation (Cohen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Basal-ganglia-recipient motor thalamus is involved in motor performance and skill learning.
source: Basal-ganglia-recipient motor thalamus, which consists of ventromedial (VM), ventral anterior and lateral (VAL) nuclei, is involved in motor performance and skill learning (Hikosaka et al., 2000; Graybiel, 2005; Turner and Desmurget, 2010; Bosch-Bouju et al., 2013; Goldberg et al., 2013; Kawai et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Activation of specific cell populations in the MLR is reinforcing.
source: Recent optogenetic studies also showed that activation of specific cell populations in the MLR (Dautan et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2016; Yoo et al., 2017) and DRN (Liu et al., 2014; McDevitt et al., 2014) is reinforcing.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Activation of specific cell populations in the DRN is reinforcing.
source: Recent optogenetic studies also showed that activation of specific cell populations in the MLR (Dautan et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2016; Yoo et al., 2017) and DRN (Liu et al., 2014; McDevitt et al., 2014) is reinforcing.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Electrical stimulation of motor thalamus supports operant behavior.
source: Additionally, electrical stimulation of motor thalamus (Clavier and Gerfen, 1982) supports operant behavior
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Lesions of motor thalamus impair striatum-dependent learning.
source: and lesions impair striatum-dependent learning (Zis et al., 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: dMSN self-stimulation was not accompanied by measurable changes in synaptic strength of excitatory afferents.
source: We found that dMSN self-stimulation was not accompanied by measurable changes in synaptic strength of excitatory afferents
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: dMSN self-stimulation was not impaired by disrupting NMDA receptors in stimulated neurons.
source: nor was it impaired by disrupting NMDA receptors in stimulated neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1h-j.

claim: Reinforcement could be elicited by direct suppression of SNr.
source: Furthermore, reinforcement could be elicited by direct suppression of SNr.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3a-c.

claim: Brainstem and thalamic targets were sufficient to drive reinforcement.
source: Although brainstem and thalamic targets were sufficient to drive reinforcement, only motor thalamus was necessary for dMSN self-stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Only motor thalamus was necessary for dMSN self-stimulation.
source: Although brainstem and thalamic targets were sufficient to drive reinforcement, only motor thalamus was necessary for dMSN self-stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: D1-ChR2 mice began to make more nosepokes on the active side and rapidly neglected the inactive nosepoke within a single session.
source: Within a single session, D1-ChR2 mice began to make more nosepokes on the active side and rapidly neglected the inactive nosepoke (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1c,d.

claim: Control mice expressing only eYFP produced fewer and equal numbers of nosepokes on both sides.
source: In contrast, control mice (expressing only eYFP) produced fewer and equal numbers of nosepokes on both sides.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1c,d.

claim: No difference in total locomotion was observed during the session.
source: Overall, no difference in total locomotion was observed during the session (Figure 1—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2f.

claim: The total number of active nosepokes per session was stable over days.
source: The total number of active nosepokes per session was stable over days (Figure 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Poking patterns did not change over time, showing stable inter-poke interval distributions and averages between day 1 and 4.
source: Similarly, poking patterns did not change over time, showing stable inter-poke interval distributions and averages between day 1 and 4.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The number of bursts and pokes/bursts did not change over days.
source: In either case, the number of bursts and pokes/bursts did not change over days (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: D1-ChR2 mice made significantly more nosepokes on the previously-active side during extinction, despite the absence of dMSN stimulation.
source: Additionally, when mice were subjected to an extinction session 24 hr after the last training session, D1-ChR2 mice made significantly more nosepokes on the previously-active side, despite the absence of dMSN stimulation (Figure 1g).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: D1-eYFP mice showed no preference for either side during extinction.
source: In contrast, D1-eYFP mice showed no preference for either side.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Behavior was learned and stabilized within a single session.
source: Together these results demonstrate that behavior was learned and stabilized within a single session
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing rapid acquisition and stable performance.

claim: Mice form a stable association (lasting at least 24 hr) between the nosepoke and the reinforcer (dMSN stimulation).
source: and that mice form a stable association (lasting at least 24 hr) between the nosepoke and the reinforcer (dMSN stimulation).
evidence: This claim is supported by the extinction data showing preference for the previously active nosepoke 24 hours later.

claim: NMDA receptors have been implicated in the induction of various forms of synaptic plasticity in the striatum.
source: NMDA receptors have been implicated in the induction of various forms of synaptic plasticity in the striatum (Calabresi et al., 1992; Thomas et al., 2000; Shen et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Interfering with striatal NMDA receptors disrupts action-outcome associations.
source: and interfering with striatal NMDA receptors disrupts action-outcome associations (Yin et al., 2005a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: D1-Cre x NR1f/f mice showed normal dMSN self-stimulation, despite a mild decrease in locomotion.
source: However, these mice showed normal dMSN self-stimulation, despite a mild decrease in locomotion (Figure 1h–j, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1h-j.

claim: No difference in mEPSC frequency or amplitude was observed in dMSNs after training.
source: We examined mEPSCs, AMPA/NMDA ratios, paired-pulse ratio, and intrinsic excitability of dMSNs, but found no difference in any of these parameters after training (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: No difference in AMPA/NMDA ratios was observed in dMSNs after training.
source: We examined mEPSCs, AMPA/NMDA ratios, paired-pulse ratio, and intrinsic excitability of dMSNs, but found no difference in any of these parameters after training (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: No difference in paired-pulse ratio was observed in dMSNs after training.
source: We examined mEPSCs, AMPA/NMDA ratios, paired-pulse ratio, and intrinsic excitability of dMSNs, but found no difference in any of these parameters after training (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: No difference in intrinsic excitability was observed in dMSNs after training.
source: We examined mEPSCs, AMPA/NMDA ratios, paired-pulse ratio, and intrinsic excitability of dMSNs, but found no difference in any of these parameters after training (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: No plastic changes were observed in synaptic transmission and excitability in iMSNs after dMSN self-stimulation.
source: Similarly, we probed synaptic transmission and excitability in iMSNs (D1-tmt negative) after dMSN self-stimulation and did not observe any plastic changes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: vGAT-Cre mice expressing Arch3.0 in the SNr learned to self-inhibit the SNr.
source: To do so, we bilaterally expressed Cre-dependent Arch3.0 in the SNr of vGAT-Cre mice. Surprisingly, these animals also learned to self-inhibit the SNr (Figure 3a–c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3a-c.

claim: Mice showed robust self-stimulation of VM.
source: Therefore, we asked whether activation of VM would be sufficient to support operant behavior. We targeted VM neurons with CaMKIIα-ChR2-containing virus in WT mice. These mice showed robust self-stimulation of VM (Figure 3d–f, Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3d-f.

claim: Self-stimulation was observed in SERT-Cre mice injected with Cre-dependent ChR2 targeting serotonergic neurons of the DRN.
source: When targeting serotonergic neurons of the DRN, we observed self-stimulation in SERT-Cre mice injected with Cre-dependent ChR2 (Figure 3g–i, Figure 1—figure supplement 1d)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3g-i.

claim: 2 of 5 mice showed clear self-stimulation behavior when targeting MLR glutamatergic neurons, whereas the other three showed no preference.
source: When placed into the operant chamber, 2 of 5 mice showed clear self-stimulation behavior, whereas the other three showed no preference (Figure 3j–l, see materials and methods for responder criterion).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3j-l.

claim: No difference in the number of nosepokes was observed between mice with lesioned or intact DRN.
source: However, we observed no difference in the number of nosepokes performed by mice with lesioned or intact DRN (Figure 4b,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4b,c.

claim: Silencing MLR glutamatergic neurons reduced dMSN-evoked locomotion.
source: We confirmed that silencing MLR glutamatergic neurons reduced dMSN-evoked locomotion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), as previously reported (Roseberry et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citation to prior work.

claim: No difference in the total number of nosepokes was observed in mice for dMSN stimulation alone or paired with inhibition of MLR glutamatergic neurons.
source: However, we observed no difference in the total number of nosepokes in mice for dMSN stimulation alone or paired with inhibition of MLR glutamatergic neurons (Figure 4e,f).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4e,f.

claim: VM-muscimol mice self-stimulated less than saline-infused control mice.
source: Overall, VM-muscimol mice self-stimulated less than saline-infused control mice (Figure 5b,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5b,c.

claim: VM silencing had no effect on either spontaneous or dMSN-evoked locomotion.
source: In contrast, VM silencing had no effect on either spontaneous or dMSN-evoked locomotion (Figure 5d,e).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5d,e.

claim: Mice made fewer nosepokes when dMSN stimulation was paired with SNr terminal stimulation in VM, compared to control mice expressing only eYFP in the SNr.
source: Similar to what we observed with muscimol infusions, mice made fewer nosepokes when dMSN stimulation was paired with SNr terminal stimulation in VM, compared to control mice expressing only eYFP in the SNr (Figure 5g,h).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5g,h.

claim: VM disinhibition is a critical component of the reinforcing circuit initiated by dMSN self-stimulation.
source: Together, these results indicate that VM disinhibition is a critical component of the reinforcing circuit initiated by dMSN self-stimulation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing VM is necessary for dMSN-driven reinforcement.

claim: An overall increase in VM activity was observed upon dMSN stimulation.
source: Consistent with the disinhibitory architecture of the basal ganglia (Deniau and Chevalier, 1985; Albin et al., 1989), we observed an overall increase in VM activity upon dMSN stimulation (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Latency to excitation in VM was short (~10–20 ms), in line with di-synaptic disinhibition via the SNr.
source: Latency to excitation was short (~10–20 ms), in line with di-synaptic disinhibition via the SNr.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6d and inference about circuit connectivity.

claim: A significant fraction of VM cells showed a decrease in firing upon dMSN stimulation.
source: However, a significant fraction of cells showed a decrease in firing, highlighting a degree of heterogeneity among VM neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: dMSN stimulation significantly increases activity in the majority of VM neurons.
source: Nevertheless, our results demonstrate that dMSN stimulation significantly increases activity in the majority of VM neurons (Figure 6), which is critical for dMSN-driven reinforcement (see below).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Silencing VM did not fully block dMSN self-stimulation.
source: Silencing VM did not fully block dMSN self-stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5 showing reduced but not eliminated self-stimulation.

claim: Mediodorsal thalamus has been implicated in action-outcome learning.
source: For example, mediodorsal thalamus, a basal ganglia-recipient, non-motor nucleus, has been implicated in action-outcome learning (Chudasama et al., 2001; Corbit et al., 2002; Corbit et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mediodorsal thalamus has been implicated in working memory.
source: and working memory (Parnaudeau et al., 2013; Bolkan et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The SNr targets the superior colliculus, which displays reward-related activity.
source: The SNr also targets the superior colliculus, which displays reward-related activity (Jeljeli et al., 2003; Doya, 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: dMSN activation may disinhibit SNc dopamine neurons and thus increase DA release, which is sufficient for reinforcement.
source: Additionally, dMSN activation, through inhibition of SNc-projecting SNr neurons (Mailly et al., 2001; Brazhnik et al., 2008), may disinhibit SNc dopamine neurons and thus increase DA release, which is sufficient for reinforcement (Phillips et al., 1976; Gratton et al., 1988; Ilango et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and speculation about circuit mechanisms.

claim: Rodent VM is embedded in circuits separate from dopamine.
source: Interestingly, rodent VM is embedded in circuits separate from dopamine (Groenewegen, 1988; Papadopoulos and Parnavelas, 1990; Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The basal ganglia could engage both dopamine-dependent and dopamine-independent reinforcement mechanisms.

source: In fact, previous reports have shown that dopamine-deficient mice can still learn to locate food in a T-maze (Robinson et al., 2005)

source: In songbirds, vocal learning requires an intact basal ganglia-thalamocortical loop (Scharff and Nottebohm, 1991; Fee and Goldberg, 2011).

claim: VM lesion studies in rodents have suggested a role for VM in spatial navigation.
source: Other lesion studies in rodents have suggested a role for VM in spatial navigation (Jeljeli et al., 2003)

source: and working memory (Bailey and Mair, 2005)

claim: VM is important for sustaining cortical motor preparatory activity in a working memory task.
source: and more specifically in sustaining cortical motor preparatory activity in a working memory task (Guo et al., 2017).

claim: VM/VAL activation increases cortical activity.

claim: VM/VAL inhibition decreases cortical activity.
source: Indeed, VM/VAL activation and inhibition increases and decreases cortical activity, respectively.

source: Thus, it appears that basal-ganglia-recipient motor thalamus may be important for engaging cortical plasticity and learning.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Basal ganglia-driven locomotion depends on MLR glutamatergic neurons, but not VM.
source: whereas basal ganglia-driven locomotion depends on MLR glutamatergic neurons, but not VM (Figure 5, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Poke rate was sensitive to laser duration.

claim: Poke rate was sensitive to stimulation pattern.
source: We characterized the self-stimulation behavior by varying different task parameters. Poke rate was sensitive to laser duration, stimulation pattern, effort, and contingency degradation, all of which are hallmarks of goal-directed behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

source: It was recently shown that VM neurons send projections to and interact with prefrontal cortices, which are involved in decision-making and learning (Kuramoto et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2017).

source: Over 1 s of stimulation, a majority of neurons were excited, while a small fraction of cells did not show any significant change in firing (Figure 6f).

source: For example, mice with dorsal striatum lesions can still learn and perform an action to obtain food rewards (Yin et al., 2005b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Altering MSN NMDAR composition by knocking out GluN2B does not prevent mice from learning a basic operant task.
source: Similarly, altering MSN NMDAR composition by knocking out GluN2B, an important subunit for plasticity induction (Paoletti et al., 2013), does not prevent mice from learning a basic operant task (Brigman et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Genetic deletion of NMDA receptors in MSNs does not prevent mice from learning simple action-outcome associations.
source: Likewise, genetic deletion of NMDA receptors in MSNs does not prevent mice from learning simple action-outcome associations (Jin and Costa, 2010); although see Beutler et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Simple forms of reinforcement may not require corticostriatal synaptic plasticity.
source: Altogether, these results are consistent with the idea that simple forms of reinforcement may not require corticostriatal synaptic plasticity, but rather take advantage of a different mechanism.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results and cited literature.

claim: DRN self-stimulation seems to rely on direct excitation of midbrain dopamine neurons.
source: Despite overall mixed observations about which exact neuronal population is sufficient for reinforcement, a common result is that DRN activation is reinforcing through direct excitation of midbrain dopamine neurons (Liu et al., 2014; McDevitt et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MLR self-stimulation of both glutamatergic and cholinergic populations seems to rely on direct excitation of midbrain dopamine neurons.
source: Similar to DRN, MLR self-stimulation of both glutamatergic and cholinergic populations seems to rely on direct excitation of midbrain dopamine neurons (Xiao et al., 2016; Yoo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: dMSN self-stimulation does not require DRN serotonergic or MLR glutamatergic neurons.
source: Altogether, these results show that dMSN self-stimulation does not require DRN serotonergic or MLR glutamatergic neurons
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: DRN and MLR belong to separate reinforcement circuits from dMSN-driven reinforcement.
source: suggesting that these nuclei belong to separate reinforcement circuits.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results.

claim: VM thalamus is traditionally classified as a motor nucleus relaying basal ganglia signals toward motor cortex.
source: VM thalamus is traditionally classified as a motor nucleus relaying basal ganglia signals toward motor cortex (Starr and Summerhayes, 1983; Klockgether et al., 1985; Turner and Desmurget, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: VM and VA/VL nuclei of the thalamus receive basal ganglia outputs.
source: VM and VA/VL nuclei of the thalamus receive basal ganglia outputs (Carter and Fibiger, 1978; Di Chiara et al., 1979)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: VM and VA/VL nuclei of the thalamus project to motor cortical regions.
